listen_text: Chapter. Epistemic Logics. Editorial note. This chapter covers the metatheory of epistemic logics. It is structured in a similar way to Aldo Antonelli's notes on classical basic modal logic, but has been rewritten by Audrey Yap in order to add material on bisimulation and dynamic epistemic logics. End editorial note.

It is structured in a similar way to Aldo Antonelli's notes on classical basic modal logic, but has been rewritten by Audrey Yap in order to add material on bisimulation and dynamic epistemic logics. End editorial note.

listen_text: Section. Introduction. Just as modal logic deals with modal propositions and the entailment relations among them, epistemic logic deals with epistemic propositions and the entailment relations among them. Rather than interpreting the modal operators as representing possibility and necessity, the unary connectives are interpreted in epistemic or doxastic ways, to model knowledge and belief. For example, we might want to express claims like the following: List. Next item. Richard knows that Calgary is in Alberta. Next item. Audrey thinks it is possible that a dog is on the couch. Next item. Richard knows that Audrey knows that her class is on Tuesdays. Next item. Everyone knows that a year has twelve months. End list. Contemporary epistemic logic is often traced to Jaako Hintikka's Knowledge and Belief, from one thousand nine hundred sixty two, and it was written at a time when possible worlds semantics were becoming increasingly more used in logic. In fact, epistemic logics use most of the same semantic tools as other modal logics, but will interpret them differently. The main change is in what we take the accessibility relation to represent. In epistemic logics, they represent some form of epistemic possibility. We'll see that the epistemic notion that we're modelling will affect the constraints that we want to place on the accessibility relation. And we'll also see what happens to correspondence theory when it is given an epistemic interpretation. You'll notice that the examples above mention two agents: Richard and Audrey, and the relationship between the things that each one knows. The epistemic logics we'll consider will be multi-agent logics, in which such things can be expressed. In contrast, a single-agent epistemic logic would only talk about what one individual knows or believes. End section.

listen_text: Section. Relational Models. The basic semantic concept for epistemic logics is the same as that of ordinary modal logics. Relational models still consist of a set of worlds, and an assignment that determines which propositional variables count as “true” at which worlds. And if we are only dealing with a single agent, we have a single accessibility relation as usual. However, if we have a multi-agent epistemic logic, then our single accessibility relation becomes a set of accessibility relations, one for each agent a in our set of agent symbols agent set G . A relational model consists of a set of worlds, which are related by binary accessibility relations—one for each agent—together with an assignment which determines which propositional variables are true at which worlds. Definition. A model for the multi-agent epistemic language is a triple model M equals the ordered triple world set W, then accessibility relation R, then valuation V , where List. Next item. world set W is a nonempty set of “worlds,” Next item. For each agent a belongs to agent set G , agent a accessibility relation R is a binary accessibility relation on world set W , and Next item. valuation V is a function assigning to each propositional variable p a set valuation V of p of possible worlds. End list. When world w prime is accessible from world w under the agent a accessibility relation holds, we say that world w prime is accessible by a from world w . When world w belongs to valuation V of p we say p is true at world w . End definition. The mechanics are just like the mechanics for normal modal logic, just with more accessibility relations added in. For a given agent, we will generally interpret their accessibility relation as representing something about their informational states. For example, we often treat world w prime is accessible from world w under the agent a accessibility relation , as expressing that world w prime is consistent with agent a apostrophe s information at world w . Or to put it another way, at world w , they cannot tell the difference between world world w and world world w prime . End section.

listen_text: Section. Truth at a World. Just as with normal modal logic, every epistemic model determines which formulas count as true at which worlds in it. We use the same notation “model model M makes formula A true at world world w ” for the basic notion of relational semantics. The relation is defined inductively and is identical to the normal modal case for all non-modal operators. Definition. Truth of a formula A at world w in a model M , in symbols: model M satisfies formula A at world w , is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is falsity. Never model M satisfies falsity at world w . Next item. model M satisfies p at world w if and only if world w belongs to valuation V of p Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy formula B at world w . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w and model M satisfies formula C at world w . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w or model M satisfies formula C at world w (or both). Next item. Case: A is the conditional from B to C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy formula B at world w or model M satisfies formula C at world w . Next item. Case: A says that agent a knows B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w prime for all world w prime belongs to world set W with world w prime is accessible from world w under the agent a accessibility relation End list. End definition. Here's where we need to think about restrictions on our accessibility relations, though. After all, by clause the knowledge clause in the definition of truth at a world , a formula agent a knows that formula B is true at world w whenever there are no world w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w under the agent a accessibility relation . This is the same clause as in normal modal logic; when a world has no successors, all the necessity operator -formulas are vacuously true there. This seems extremely counterintuitive if we think about the single-agent knowledge operator as representing knowledge. After all, we tend to think that there are no circumstances under which an agent might know both formula A and not formula A at the same time. One solution is to ensure that our accessibility relation in epistemic logic will always be reflexive. This roughly corresponds to the idea that the actual world is consistent with an agent's information. In fact, epistemic logics typically use Sfive, but others might use weaker systems depending on what exactly they want the the knowledge operator for agent a relation to represent. Figure. listen_text: Section. Accessibility Relations and Epistemic Principles. Given what we already know about frame correspondence in normal modal logics, we might want to see what the characteristic formulas look like given epistemic interpretations. We have already said that epistemic logics are typically interpreted in Sfive. So let's take a look at how various epistemic principles are represented, and consider how they correspond to various frame conditions. Recall from normal modal logic, that different modal formulas characterized different properties of accessibility relations. This table picks out a few that correspond to particular epistemic principles. Table. t. Epistemic correspondence table. Column headers: if accessibility relation R has the stated property; then the displayed principle is true in model M . Row one has an intentionally blank frame-condition cell; Closure: if it is known that p implies q, then, if p is known, q is known . Row two, reflexive: for every world w, w is accessible from itself under relation R ; Veridicality: if p is known, then p is true . Row three, transitive: for every u, v, and w, if v is accessible from u and w is accessible from v, then w is accessible from u ; Positive Introspection: if p is known, then it is known that p is known . Row four, euclidean: for every w, u, and v, if u and v are each accessible from w, then v is accessible from u ; Negative Introspection: if p is not known, then it is known that p is not known . End table. Caption. Four epistemic principles. End caption. End table. Veridicality, corresponding to the axiom T axiom, is often treated as the most uncontroversial of these principles, as it represents that claim that if a formula is known, then it must be true. Closure, as well as Positive and Negative Introspection are much more contested. Closure, corresponding to the axiom K axiom, represents the idea that an agent's knowledge is closed under implication. This might seem plausible to us in some cases. For instance, I might know that if I am in Victoria, then I am on Vancouver Island. Barring odd skeptical scenarios, I do know that I am in Victoria, and this should also suggest that I know I am on Vancouver Island. So in this case, the logical closure of my knowledge might seem relatively intuitive. On the other hand, we do not always think through the consequences of our knowledge, and so this might lead to less intuitive results in other cases. Positive Introspection, sometimes known as the KK-principle, is sometimes articulated as the statement that if I know something, then I know that I know. It is the epistemic counterpart of the four axiom. Correspondingly, negative introspection is articulated as the statement that if I don't know something, then I know that I don't know it, which is the counterpart of the five axiom. Both of these seem to admit of relatively ordinary counterexamples, in which I am unsure whether or not I know something that I do in fact know. End section.

text: Section. Accessibility Relations and Epistemic Principles. Given what we already know about frame correspondence in normal modal logics, we might want to see what the characteristic formulas look like given epistemic interpretations. We have already said that epistemic logics are typically interpreted in Sfive. So let's take a look at how various epistemic principles are represented, and consider how they correspond to various frame conditions. Recall from normal modal logic, that different modal formulas characterized different properties of accessibility relations. This table picks out a few that correspond to particular epistemic principles. Table. t. Epistemic correspondence table. Column headers: if accessibility relation R has the stated property; then the displayed principle is true in model M . Row one has an intentionally blank frame-condition cell; Closure: if it is known that p implies q, then, if p is known, q is known . Row two, reflexive: for every world w, w is accessible from itself under relation R ; Veridicality: if p is known, then p is true . Row three, transitive: for every u, v, and w, if v is accessible from u and w is accessible from v, then w is accessible from u ; Positive Introspection: if p is known, then it is known that p is known . Row four, euclidean: for every w, u, and v, if u and v are each accessible from w, then v is accessible from u ; Negative Introspection: if p is not known, then it is known that p is not known . End table. Caption. Four epistemic principles. End caption. End table. Veridicality, corresponding to the axiom T axiom, is often treated as the most uncontroversial of these principles, as it represents that claim that if a formula is known, then it must be true. Closure, as well as Positive and Negative Introspection are much more contested. Closure, corresponding to the axiom K axiom, represents the idea that an agent's knowledge is closed under implication. This might seem plausible to us in some cases. For instance, I might know that if I am in Victoria, then I am on Vancouver Island. Barring odd skeptical scenarios, I do know that I am in Victoria, and this should also suggest that I know I am on Vancouver Island. So in this case, the logical closure of my knowledge might seem relatively intuitive. On the other hand, we do not always think through the consequences of our knowledge, and so this might lead to less intuitive results in other cases. Positive Introspection, sometimes known as the KK-principle, is sometimes articulated as the statement that if I know something, then I know that I know. It is the epistemic counterpart of the four axiom. Correspondingly, negative introspection is articulated as the statement that if I don't know something, then I know that I don't know it, which is the counterpart of the five axiom. Both of these seem to admit of relatively ordinary counterexamples, in which I am unsure whether or not I know something that I do in fact know. End section.

listen_text: Section. Bisimulations. One remaining question that we might have about the expressive power of our epistemic language has to do with the relationship between models and the formulas that hold in them. We have seen from our frame correspondence results that when certain formulas are valid in a frame, they will also ensure that those frames satisfy certain properties. But does our modal language, for example, allow us to distinguish between a world at which there is a reflexive arrow, and an infinite chain of worlds, each of which leads to the next? That is, is there any formula A that might hold at only one of these two worlds? Bisimulation is a relationship that we can define between relational models to say that they have effectively the same structure. And as we will see, it will capture a sense of equivalence between models that can be captured in our epistemic language. Definition. Bisimulation. We say that bisimulation relation script R is a bisimulation when for every the ordered pair world w subscript one, then world w subscript two belongs to bisimulation relation script R , we have: List. Next item. world w subscript one belongs to valuation V subscript one of p if and only if world w subscript two belongs to valuation V subscript two of p for all propositional variables p . For all agents agent a belongs to agent set A and worlds world v subscript one belongs to world set W subscript one , if world v subscript one is accessible from world w subscript one under the agent a accessibility relation in model one then there is some world v subscript two belongs to world set W subscript two such that world v subscript two is accessible from world w subscript two under the agent a accessibility relation in model two , and the ordered pair world v subscript one, then world v subscript two belongs to bisimulation relation script R . Many of these represent changes in knowlege using informational events or updates. The most basic kind of update is a public announcement in which some formula is truthfully announced and all of the agents witness this taking place together. However, the semantics for the public announcement operator are something new. Definition. Truth of a formula A at world w in a model M equals the ordered triple world set W, then accessibility relation R, then valuation V , in symbols: model M satisfies formula A at world w , is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is falsity. Never model M satisfies falsity at world w . Next item. model M satisfies p at world w if and only if world w belongs to valuation V of p Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy formula B at world w . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w and model M satisfies formula C at world w . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w or model M satisfies formula C at world w (or both). Next item. We can see the public announcement of a formula as shrinking a model, or restricting it to the worlds at which the formula was true. the before-and-after public-announcement model gives an example of the effects of publicly announcing p . One notable thing about that model is that agent agent b learns that p as a result of the announcement, while agent agent a does not (since agent a already knew that p was true). In fact, it is the case that model M satisfies after p is truthfully announced, it is common knowledge among the group containing agent a and agent b that p holds at world w subscript one . In other words, after p is announced, it becomes common knowledge. We might wonder, though, whether this holds in the general case, and whether a truthful announcement of formula A will always result in formula A becoming common knowledge. It may be surprising that the answer is no. And in fact, it is possible to truthfully announce formulas that will no longer be true once they are announced. Therefore, model M restricted by open scope, p and not agent b knows that p, close scope satisfies not open scope, p and not agent b knows that p, close scope at world w prime subscript one , so this is a formula that becomes false once it has been announced. text: Section. Semantics of Public Announcement Logic. Relational models for public announcement logics are the same as they were in epistemic logics. However, the semantics for the public announcement operator are something new. Definition. Truth of a formula A at world w in a model M equals the ordered triple world set W, then accessibility relation R, then valuation V , in symbols: model M satisfies formula A at world w , is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is falsity. Never model M satisfies falsity at world w . Next item. model M satisfies p at world w if and only if world w belongs to valuation V of p Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy formula B at world w . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w and model M satisfies formula C at world w . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w or model M satisfies formula C at world w (or both). Next item. Case: A says that after B is truthfully announced, C holds. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies formula B at world w implies model M restricted by formula B satisfies formula C at world w Where model M restricted by formula B equals the ordered triple remaining world set W prime, then accessibility relation R prime, then valuation V prime is defined as follows: List. Next item. remaining world set W prime equals the set of all world u in world set W such that model M satisfies formula B at world u . So the worlds of model M restricted by formula B are the worlds in model M at which formula B holds. Next item. agent a accessibility relation R prime equals agent a accessibility relation R intersected with open scope, remaining world set W prime cross remaining world set W prime, close scope . Each agent's accessibility relation is simply restricted to the worlds that remain in remaining world set W prime . Next item. valuation V prime of p equals the set of all world u in remaining world set W prime such that world u belongs to valuation V of p . Similarly, the propositional valuations at worlds remain the same, representing the idea that informational events will not change the truth value of propositional variables. End list. End list. End definition. What is distinctive, then, about public announcement logics, is that the truth of a formula at model M can sometimes only be decided by referring to a model other than model M itself. Notice also that our semantics treats the announcement operator as a the necessity operator operator, and so if a formula A cannot be truthfully announced at a world, then after formula A is truthfully announced, formula B holds will hold there trivially, just as all the necessity operator formulas hold at endpoints. We can see the public announcement of a formula as shrinking a model, or restricting it to the worlds at which the formula was true. the before-and-after public-announcement model gives an example of the effects of publicly announcing p . One notable thing about that model is that agent agent b learns that p as a result of the announcement, while agent agent a does not (since agent a already knew that p was true). More formally, we have model M satisfies not agent b knows that p at world w subscript one but model M restricted by p satisfies agent b knows that p at world w prime subscript one . This implies that model M satisfies after p is truthfully announced, agent b knows that p holds at world w subscript one . But we have some even stronger claims that we can make about the result of the announcement. In fact, it is the case that model M satisfies after p is truthfully announced, it is common knowledge among the group containing agent a and agent b that p holds at world w subscript one . In other words, after p is announced, it becomes common knowledge. We might wonder, though, whether this holds in the general case, and whether a truthful announcement of formula A will always result in formula A becoming common knowledge. It may be surprising that the answer is no. And in fact, it is possible to truthfully announce formulas that will no longer be true once they are announced. For example, consider the effects of announcing p and not agent b knows that p at world w subscript one in the before-and-after public-announcement model . In fact, model M restricted by p and model M restricted by open scope, p and not agent b knows that p, close scope are the same model. However, as we have already noted, model M restricted by p satisfies agent b knows that p at world w prime subscript one . Therefore, model M restricted by open scope, p and not agent b knows that p, close scope satisfies not open scope, p and not agent b knows that p, close scope at world w prime subscript one , so this is a formula that becomes false once it has been announced.
